focus: Exodus 25 begins the LORD’s instructions on the mountain for a sanctuary built from the people’s willing offerings, “that I may dwell among them” (Exodus 25:8). He gives Moses the pattern for the first furnishings, starting with the ark and mercy seat where He will meet with Moses, then the table for the showbread and the golden lampstand.

sections.title: A Sanctuary from Willing Hearts So the LORD May Dwell Among Them
sections.summary: The LORD asks for an offering from everyone “who gives it willingly with his heart” (Exodus 25:2), naming the metals, cloth, skins, wood, oil, spices, and stones to be given. He states His purpose, “let them make Me a sanctuary, that I may dwell among them” (Exodus 25:8), and commands that it be made according to the pattern He shows Moses.

sections.title: The Ark and the Mercy Seat Where God Will Meet with Moses
sections.summary: Israel is to make an ark of acacia wood overlaid with gold, carried by poles that are never removed, and to place the Testimony inside it. Over it they are to set a mercy seat of pure gold with two cherubim of one piece with it, where the LORD promises, “there I will meet with you, and I will speak with you” (Exodus 25:22).

sections.title: The Table for the Showbread
sections.summary: Israel is to make a table of acacia wood overlaid with gold, with rings and poles for carrying it and dishes, pans, pitchers, and bowls of pure gold. On it they are to “set the showbread on the table before Me always” (Exodus 25:30).

sections.title: The Golden Lampstand and the Pattern Shown on the Mountain
sections.summary: Israel is to make a lampstand of one hammered piece of pure gold, with six branches and bowls like almond blossoms, and seven lamps to give light in front of it. Moses is charged, “see to it that you make them according to the pattern which was shown you on the mountain” (Exodus 25:40).

1.brief: The LORD speaks to Moses on the mountain. The instructions for the sanctuary begin with God’s own word.
1.explain:
“Then the LORD spoke to Moses, saying:”

Moses is on the mountain in the cloud (24:18). God now gives him the instructions for the sanctuary, which run through 31:18.

2.brief: Israel is to bring God an offering, taken “From everyone who gives it willingly with his heart.” God’s dwelling will be built from gifts freely given.
2.explain:
“Speak to the children of Israel, that they bring Me an offering.”

God asks His people for “an offering.” The Hebrew word describes something lifted up or set apart as a contribution to God.

“From everyone who gives it willingly with his heart you shall take My offering.”

The gift is to come only from those who give “willingly with his heart.” The materials listed in this chapter were to come from these freely given gifts. The census ransom in 30:11–16 was different: a required half shekel from each counted man, which later supplied the silver sockets and fittings of the sanctuary (38:25–28). When the time came, the people gave so much that Moses had to stop them (36:5–7).

3.brief: The offering is to include gold, silver, and bronze. The materials come from what the people possess.
3.explain:
“And this is the offering which you shall take from them: gold, silver, and bronze;”

The metals come first: “gold, silver, and bronze.” Much of this likely came from what the Egyptians gave Israel at the exodus (12:35–36).

4.brief: The offering also includes blue, purple, and scarlet thread, fine linen, and goats’ hair. These materials will form the sanctuary’s fabrics and coverings.
4.explain:
“blue, purple, and scarlet thread, fine linen, and goats’ hair;”

The fabrics follow. “Blue, purple, and scarlet” were costly dyed threads. “Fine linen” was the finest Egyptian cloth. “Goats’ hair” was woven into durable tent cloth.

5.brief: Ram skins dyed red, badger skins, and acacia wood are also to be given. The list provides for the outer coverings and the wooden frame.
5.explain:
“ram skins dyed red, badger skins, and acacia wood;”

These provided the outer coverings and the wooden frame. “Acacia wood” grew in the Sinai desert and is hard and durable.
5.notes: The Hebrew word translated “badger skins” is uncertain. Suggestions include the skins of sea animals such as dugongs, or fine leather.

6.brief: Oil for the light and spices for the anointing oil and incense complete the supplies for worship. The offering provides for the ongoing service of the sanctuary.
6.explain:
“oil for the light, and spices for the anointing oil and for the sweet incense;”

Some gifts would be used up in ongoing worship: “oil for the light” and “spices” for the anointing oil and incense (30:22–38).

7.brief: Onyx stones and stones for the ephod and breastplate are to be given. Even the priest’s garments will come from the people’s gifts.
7.explain:
“onyx stones, and stones to be set in the ephod and in the breastplate.”

Precious stones were needed for the high priest’s garments (28:9–21). Even the priest’s garments would come from the people’s gifts.

8.brief: “And let them make Me a sanctuary, that I may dwell among them.” God’s purpose in the whole project is to live among His people.
8.explain:
“And let them make Me a sanctuary,”

A “sanctuary” is a holy place, set apart for God.

“that I may dwell among them.”

This is the purpose of everything that follows. God wants to “dwell among them.” The God who brought Israel out of Egypt to Himself (19:4) now commands a dwelling so that He can live in their midst. John 1:14 says, “the Word became flesh and dwelt among us,” using a Greek verb that means to pitch a tent. In Christ, God came to dwell with His people, and Revelation 21:3 looks to the day when “the tabernacle of God is with men, and He will dwell with them.”
8.notes: The Hebrew verb for “dwell” (shakan) is related to the word for the tabernacle (mishkan), the dwelling place.

9.brief: Israel is to make it exactly according to the pattern of the tabernacle and its furnishings that God shows Moses. The design comes from God, not from human imagination, and Hebrews 8:5 calls it a copy of heavenly things.
9.explain:
“According to all that I show you, that is, the pattern of the tabernacle and the pattern of all its furnishings,”

God shows Moses “the pattern,” a model or plan for the tabernacle and its furnishings.

“just so you shall make it.”

Israel must build it “just so,” exactly as God showed. The design comes from God, not from human imagination. Hebrews 8:5 says the priests “serve the copy and shadow of the heavenly things, as Moses was divinely instructed when he was about to make the tabernacle.” The earthly sanctuary pointed beyond itself to heavenly realities fulfilled in Christ.

10.brief: Israel is to make an ark of acacia wood, two and a half cubits long and a cubit and a half wide and high. The instructions begin with the most important furnishing.
10.explain:
“And they shall make an ark of acacia wood;”

The instructions begin with the most important furnishing, “an ark,” a chest or box. It would stand in the Most Holy Place.

“two and a half cubits shall be its length, a cubit and a half its width, and a cubit and a half its height.”

A cubit was about 18 inches, the length from elbow to fingertip. The ark was roughly 45 inches long, 27 inches wide, and 27 inches high.

11.brief: The ark is overlaid with pure gold inside and out, with a gold molding around it. The ark is made fitting for the holy presence of God.
11.explain:
“And you shall overlay it with pure gold, inside and out you shall overlay it,”

The ark is covered with “pure gold” inside and outside. It is made fitting for the holy presence of God.

“and shall make on it a molding of gold all around.”

A gold “molding,” a rim or border, runs around the top.

12.brief: Four gold rings are cast for its four corners, two on each side. The rings prepare the ark to be carried.
12.explain:
“You shall cast four rings of gold for it, and put them in its four corners;”

Four “rings of gold” are attached at the corners, probably near the feet.

“two rings shall be on one side, and two rings on the other side.”

The rings prepare the ark to be carried.

13.brief: Poles of acacia wood are made and overlaid with gold. The ark will be carried by poles, not by hand.
13.explain:
“And you shall make poles of acacia wood, and overlay them with gold.”

Gold-covered “poles” will be used to carry the ark.

14.brief: The poles are put through the rings on the sides of the ark so that it can be carried. The ark is designed to travel with Israel.
14.explain:
“You shall put the poles into the rings on the sides of the ark, that the ark may be carried by them.”

The ark is to be “carried” by poles, not touched by hand. The ark is designed to travel with Israel.
14.notes: When the ark was later moved on a cart and Uzzah touched it, God struck him (2 Samuel 6:6–7). David then had the Levites carry it on poles as Moses commanded (1 Chronicles 15:13–15).

15.brief: The poles must stay in the rings and never be removed. The ark is always ready to move with God’s people.
15.explain:
“The poles shall be in the rings of the ark; they shall not be taken from it.”

The poles must stay in place permanently. The ark is always ready to move with God’s people.

16.brief: The Testimony that God will give is to be put inside the ark. The ark will hold the tablets of God’s covenant.
16.explain:
“And you shall put into the ark the Testimony which I will give you.”

“The Testimony” refers to the two stone tablets of the law (31:18). They witness to God’s covenant with Israel. The ark will hold the tablets of God’s covenant.
16.notes: Hebrews 9:4 says the ark also held the golden pot of manna and Aaron’s rod that budded (16:33–34; Numbers 17:10). By Solomon’s time only the tablets remained (1 Kings 8:9).

17.brief: Israel is to make a mercy seat of pure gold, the same length and width as the ark. The mercy seat will cover the ark and become the place of meeting.
17.explain:
“You shall make a mercy seat of pure gold;”

The “mercy seat” is the lid or cover of the ark, made of solid gold. The Hebrew word comes from a root meaning to cover or to make atonement. On the Day of Atonement the high priest sprinkled blood on it (Leviticus 16:14–15).

“two and a half cubits shall be its length and a cubit and a half its width.”

It is the same size as the ark. The mercy seat will cover the ark and become the place of meeting.
17.notes: The Greek translation uses the word hilasterion for the mercy seat. Paul uses the same word of Christ, “whom God set forth as a propitiation by His blood” (Romans 3:25). Hebrews 9:5 refers to the cherubim “overshadowing the mercy seat.”

18.brief: Two cherubim of hammered gold are made at the two ends of the mercy seat. The following verses describe how they are joined to the mercy seat and how they face.
18.explain:
“And you shall make two cherubim of gold;”

“Cherubim” are heavenly beings who guard God’s holiness. They first appear guarding the way to the tree of life (Genesis 3:24).

“of hammered work you shall make them at the two ends of the mercy seat.”

They are beaten from gold, one at each end of the mercy seat.

19.brief: The cherubim are made of one piece with the mercy seat, one at each end. The cherubim and mercy seat form one whole.
19.explain:
“Make one cherub at one end, and the other cherub at the other end;”

One cherub stands at each end.

“you shall make the cherubim at the two ends of it of one piece with the mercy seat.”

The cherubim are hammered “of one piece with the mercy seat.” The cherubim and mercy seat form one whole.

20.brief: The cherubim stretch out their wings above, covering the mercy seat, and face one another toward it. Their posture directs attention to the mercy seat.
20.explain:
“And the cherubim shall stretch out their wings above, covering the mercy seat with their wings,”

Their wings spread “above,” sheltering “the mercy seat.”

“and they shall face one another; the faces of the cherubim shall be toward the mercy seat.”

They face each other and look down “toward the mercy seat.” Their posture directs attention to the mercy seat, the place of God’s presence and atonement.

21.brief: The mercy seat is placed on top of the ark, and the Testimony is put inside. The covenant law lies beneath the mercy seat.
21.explain:
“You shall put the mercy seat on top of the ark, and in the ark you shall put the Testimony that I will give you.”

The mercy seat covers the ark, and the tablets lie inside. The covenant law lies beneath the mercy seat. Between the holy God and the law Israel would break stood the place where atonement would be made.

22.brief: “And there I will meet with you, and I will speak with you from above the mercy seat,” from between the cherubim, about all His commands for Israel. The mercy seat is the place where God will meet and speak with Moses.
22.explain:
“And there I will meet with you,”

The mercy seat is the place of meeting between God and His people’s mediator.

“and I will speak with you from above the mercy seat, from between the two cherubim which are on the ark of the Testimony,”

God’s voice will come from the space above the ark, framed by the cherubim. Numbers 7:89 records that Moses heard God’s voice there.

“about everything which I will give you in commandment to the children of Israel.”

From there God will give His commands for Israel. The mercy seat is the place where God will meet and speak with Moses. Hebrews shows Christ entering heaven itself with His own blood and so giving His people access to God (Hebrews 9:11–14, 24).
22.notes: Scripture often speaks of God as enthroned above the cherubim (1 Samuel 4:4; Psalm 80:1; 99:1). The ark served as His footstool (1 Chronicles 28:2).

23.brief: Israel is to make a table of acacia wood, two cubits long, a cubit wide, and a cubit and a half high. The second furnishing will hold bread before the LORD.
23.explain:
“You shall also make a table of acacia wood;”

The second furnishing is “a table” for the holy place.

“two cubits shall be its length, a cubit its width, and a cubit and a half its height.”

It was about 36 inches long, 18 inches wide, and 27 inches high. The table will hold bread before the LORD.

24.brief: The table is overlaid with pure gold and given a gold molding around it. Like the ark, it is fitted for God’s presence.
24.explain:
“And you shall overlay it with pure gold, and make a molding of gold all around.”

Like the ark, the table is overlaid with “pure gold” and given a gold “molding.”

25.brief: A frame a handbreadth wide is made around it, with a gold molding for the frame. The details complete the table’s form.
25.explain:
“You shall make for it a frame of a handbreadth all around,”

A “frame” or rim about three inches wide runs around the table, perhaps to keep items from sliding off.

“and you shall make a gold molding for the frame all around.”

The frame also has a gold molding.

26.brief: Four gold rings are made and placed at the four corners by its legs. The table, like the ark, is prepared for carrying.
26.explain:
“And you shall make for it four rings of gold, and put the rings on the four corners that are at its four legs.”

Four gold rings are fixed at the corners by the legs. The table, like the ark, is prepared for carrying.

27.brief: The rings are close to the frame as holders for the poles. The arrangement allows the table to travel with Israel.
27.explain:
“The rings shall be close to the frame, as holders for the poles to bear the table.”

The rings hold the carrying poles.

28.brief: Poles of acacia wood overlaid with gold are made for carrying the table. The table will move with the sanctuary.
28.explain:
“And you shall make the poles of acacia wood, and overlay them with gold, that the table may be carried with them.”

Gold-covered poles are made for carrying. The table will move with the sanctuary.

29.brief: Its dishes, pans, pitchers, and bowls for pouring are made of pure gold. The utensils for the table’s service are as precious as the table itself.
29.explain:
“You shall make its dishes, its pans, its pitchers, and its bowls for pouring.”

The table has its utensils: “dishes,” “pans,” “pitchers,” and “bowls for pouring,” probably for drink offerings.

“You shall make them of pure gold.”

They too are “of pure gold.” The utensils for the table’s service are as precious as the table itself.

30.brief: “And you shall set the showbread on the table before Me always.” Bread is to be kept continually in the LORD’s presence.
30.explain:
“And you shall set the showbread on the table before Me always.”

“The showbread,” literally bread of the presence, is to be on the table “before Me always.” Leviticus 24:5–9 describes twelve loaves, one for each tribe, replaced every Sabbath and eaten by the priests. Bread is kept continually in the LORD’s presence. The table and its bread picture Christ, who nourishes His people. John 6 first speaks of the manna, and then Jesus says, “I am the bread of life” (John 6:35). The showbread keeps its own setting in the sanctuary, where the bread stood before God for all twelve tribes.
30.notes: David and his men ate the showbread when they were hungry (1 Samuel 21:1–6). Jesus cited that event when He defended His disciples (Matthew 12:3–4).

31.brief: Israel is to make a lampstand of pure hammered gold, with its shaft, branches, bowls, knobs, and flowers all of one piece. The lampstand is made as a single crafted piece.
31.explain:
“You shall also make a lampstand of pure gold; the lampstand shall be of hammered work.”

The third furnishing is “a lampstand” for the holy place. It is hammered from “pure gold.”

“Its shaft, its branches, its bowls, its ornamental knobs, and flowers shall be of one piece.”

Every part is “of one piece.” The lampstand is made as a single crafted piece.
31.notes: The Hebrew word for lampstand is menorah.

32.brief: Six branches come out of its sides, three on each side. The branches spread its light.
32.explain:
“And six branches shall come out of its sides:”

“Six branches” extend from the central shaft.

“three branches of the lampstand out of one side, and three branches of the lampstand out of the other side.”

Three on each side, with the shaft in the center, make seven lamps. The branches spread its light.

33.brief: Each branch has three bowls shaped like almond blossoms, each with a knob and a flower. The lampstand is shaped like a flowering tree.
33.explain:
“Three bowls shall be made like almond blossoms on one branch, with an ornamental knob and a flower,”

Each branch has “three bowls” shaped “like almond blossoms,” with a knob and flower.

“and three bowls made like almond blossoms on the other branch, with an ornamental knob and a flower—and so for the six branches that come out of the lampstand.”

The pattern repeats on all six branches. The lampstand is shaped like a flowering tree.
33.notes: The almond tree blossoms early in the year. Aaron’s rod later budded and bore almonds as a sign of God’s choice (Numbers 17:8). The Hebrew word for almond is related to a word meaning to watch or be awake (Jeremiah 1:11–12).

34.brief: The central shaft has four almond-blossom bowls with their knobs and flowers. The main stem is more richly ornamented than the branches.
34.explain:
“On the lampstand itself four bowls shall be made like almond blossoms, each with its ornamental knob and flower.”

The central shaft has “four bowls.” The main stem is more richly ornamented than the branches.

35.brief: A knob is placed under each pair of branches where they come out of the shaft. The design unites the branches with the central stem.
35.explain:
“And there shall be a knob under the first two branches of the same, a knob under the second two branches of the same, and a knob under the third two branches of the same,”

A knob sits under each pair of branches where they leave the shaft.

“according to the six branches that extend from the lampstand.”

The design unites the branches with the central stem.

36.brief: All the knobs and branches are one hammered piece of pure gold. The whole lampstand is a single work.
36.explain:
“Their knobs and their branches shall be of one piece; all of it shall be one hammered piece of pure gold.”

Everything is “one hammered piece of pure gold.” The whole lampstand is a single work.

37.brief: Seven lamps are made and arranged to give light in front of it. The lampstand’s purpose is to give light in the holy place.
37.explain:
“You shall make seven lamps for it,”

“Seven lamps” sit on top of the shaft and branches.

“and they shall arrange its lamps so that they give light in front of it.”

The lamps are arranged to “give light in front of it.” The holy place had no windows. The lampstand was its only light. Its purpose was to give light in the holy place. The lampstand pictures Christ, who gives His people light. Jesus said, “I am the light of the world. He who follows Me shall not walk in darkness, but have the light of life” (John 8:12).

38.brief: Its wick-trimmers and their trays are made of pure gold. Even the tools for tending the lamps are of gold.
38.explain:
“And its wick-trimmers and their trays shall be of pure gold.”

Even the “wick-trimmers” and “trays” for the burned wicks are of gold.

39.brief: The lampstand and all its utensils are made from a talent of pure gold. The lampstand is costly and precious.
39.explain:
“It shall be made of a talent of pure gold, with all these utensils.”

A “talent” was about 75 pounds. The lampstand and its tools were costly and precious.

40.brief: “And see to it that you make them according to the pattern which was shown you on the mountain.” Moses must follow God’s pattern exactly, and Hebrews 8:5 quotes this verse.
40.explain:
“And see to it that you make them according to the pattern which was shown you on the mountain.”

God repeats the warning of 25:9. Moses must “see to it” that everything follows “the pattern.” Moses must follow God’s pattern exactly. Hebrews 8:5 quotes this verse to show that the earthly sanctuary was a copy of heavenly things.
